## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Mūsikajātaka* (Ja 373), translated as *The Tale of Mūsikā*, is a narrative belonging to the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral]. According to the canonical framework, the Buddha delivered this discourse while residing at the Bamboo Grove (Veḷuvana) near Rājagaha concerning King Ajātasattu [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1883]. Observing the king playing with his young son while listening to the Dhamma, the Buddha discerned that the boy would bring mortal danger to his father, remarking that prudent monarchs of old kept suspicious heirs in confinement until their own funerals [SuttaCentral]. The introductory narrative links this sermon directly to the events recounted in the *Thusajātaka* [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1883]. In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta was a world-renowned teacher (*disāpāmokkhācariya*) who perceived through divination that a royal student faced peril from his offspring; he composed a verse beginning *Kuhiṃ gatā kattha gatā ti* based on an incident in which a wounded horse struck and killed a bothersome mouse (*mūsikā*) into a well [Fausböll 1883].
Scholarly analysis situates the *Mūsikajātaka*, alongside the *Thusajātaka* and *Saṃkiccajātaka*, within a group of Jātaka tales illustrating previous births associated with Ajātasattu [Radich 2011]. These stories explore the theme of patricide and share the common motif of princes whose plots against their royal fathers are thwarted through the prescient warnings of a wise advisor [Radich 2011].
DharmaNexus identifies extensive Pali-internal text reuse between the canonical text and seven segments of the prose commentary in the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Vol. 3) [DharmaNexus]. Neither SuttaCentral nor DharmaNexus records any external cross-language parallels in Sanskrit, Tibetan, or Chinese corpora; SuttaCentral lists four modern translations across four languages [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus].
